findings: The prompt repeatedly treats an incomplete or fragmentary prefix (a piece that lacks the finishing verb, complement, or reported content) as if it were a high-probability contradiction of the whole sentence. In many cases the prefix is merely incomplete (a cohesion problem) rather than asserting something the rest of the sentence contradicts; the prompt therefore over-allocates 'contra' mass to fragmentation and overturns good dense segmentations.

The prompt conflates speech-act or reporting verbs and left fragments that name an act ('erklärten', 'wurden', 'belegt', 'wurden am ... gezwungen') with contradicted factual assertions. It therefore assigns large contradiction probability to prefixes that report an act but do not assert propositional content; this routinely kills otherwise acceptable cuts.

findings: The prompt systematically underestimates contradiction risk when a cut leaves a prefix that reads like an independent assertion because it ends on a finite/reporting verb or other predicate‑like material without its resolving complement, so high‑contra cuts are ranked too high.

diagnosis.why: The inserted special-case penalised cuts that leave the left fragment ending on a finite/reporting verb, so the scorer shifted cuts away from verb-final prefixes (e.g. merged 'Schlafen ‖ Sie' into 'Schlafen Sie ...' and kept verb+object together). That change helped the smallest-piece bin (≤3 pieces: +0.0092) but displaced cuts into other boundaries—sometimes splitting named entities and enumerations (e.g. 'Mission Bay' was split)—producing net small harms in the mid/longer bins (≤5: −0.0161, ≤10: −0.0054) and nearly balanced n_worse/n_better.
diagnosis.lesson: A later revision should respect that penalising predicate-ending prefixes helps very short-piece cuts but can push cuts into names/enumerations and hurt mid-length cases, so its scope must be constrained to avoid creating those splits.

changelog: Insert a new Core Principle directing the scorer to prefer very-early cuts after initial clause-introducers when safe and to make predicate-ending penalties explicitly conditional on the remainder containing clause-level qualifiers/negation/scope carriers — this addresses the primary finding that a blanket predicate-ending penalty and underweighting of clause-introducers harmed mid-length bins.
findings: The scorer systematically undervalues very-early, dense cuts immediately after clause-introducing particles and initial subordinators (e.g. 'Wenn man', 'Auch wenn', initial adverbials). Those prefixes are often the safest place to cut because they isolate the clause introducer and prevent the left fragment from asserting a claim later reversed or qualified — ask: does the remainder contain an explicit qualification/negation that would reverse the prefix? If not, prefer the early cut.

The prompt applies a blanket penalty to cuts that leave the left fragment ending on a finite verb or 'predicate-ending' prefix. Applied globally, this shifts cuts into names and enumerations and harms mid-length bins. The correct judgement is conditional: penalize predicate-ending prefixes only when the right-hand remainder contains clause-level qualifiers/negation or scope carriers that would change the left fragment's asserted meaning; do not forbid dense cuts inside names/enumerations or short chunks when no such clause-level reversal exists.
